title: Dexterous Manipulation for Lab Automation
summary: Building data and perception pipelines to support dexterous robot manipulation in clinical-lab-style tasks.
challenge: Human hands are remarkably capable at manipulating small, delicate objects. Transferring that dexterity to robots requires precise motion data, robust perception, and careful interaction with the physical world.
overview: In the LIDAR Lab, I contribute to research on robot manipulation for clinical laboratory workflows. My work connects multi-camera calibration, motion capture, gloved-hand data collection, and trajectory processing to support learning and evaluation of manipulation behaviors. This is ongoing research; the site does not claim a completed end-to-end autonomous system.
contributions: Work on multi-camera and motion-capture calibration for synchronized hand-motion data collection.
Process raw recordings into more stable marker and hand-pose trajectories for downstream learning.
Explore 3D hand appearance reconstruction and segmentation tools to help interpret hand-object interactions.
Support simulation and evaluation workflows for manipulation subtasks involving laboratory objects.
workflow: Capture
Collect synchronized visual and motion-capture observations of human manipulation.
Recover
Calibrate sensors and process marker and hand-pose trajectories into a usable representation.
Learn & evaluate
Use processed demonstrations and simulation experiments to investigate robot manipulation behaviors.
takeaway: Current focus: improving the reliability of real-world demonstrations and their usefulness for dexterous robot learning.

title: Learning Bimanual Dexterity from Human Videos
summary: Reconstructing simulation-ready scenes from videos to explore learning bimanual robot behaviors.
challenge: Robotic learning from human videos needs more than visual imitation: a system must recover the geometry, object interactions, and physical structure of a scene so that robot behaviors can be evaluated in simulation.
overview: In the STAR Lab, I work on real-to-sim scene reconstruction as part of a broader video-to-sim-to-real research direction. The goal is to convert observations of human activities into structured, simulation-ready scenes that can support robot-policy learning and evaluation. Deployment to real robots is a research objective, not an outcome claimed here.
contributions: Contribute to scene reconstruction pipelines that recover objects and spatial layout from videos.
Assemble and validate simulation environments, including geometry, object relationships, and physics properties.
Use Isaac Sim / Isaac Lab workflows to inspect reconstructed scenes and robot interactions.
Investigate ways to make the reconstruction and validation pipeline more efficient.
workflow: Observe
Analyze visual evidence and extract the scene elements relevant to the demonstrated task.
Reconstruct
Recover usable 3D geometry, poses and object representations for a simulator.
Simulate
Validate scene interactions and explore policy-learning evaluations for bimanual manipulation.
takeaway: Current focus: making reconstructed environments more reliable and quicker to validate, so they can serve as useful testbeds for embodied learning.

title: Radar–Camera Fusion for Field-Robot Perception
summary: Combining a monocular camera and 77 GHz mmWave radar to enrich object detection for field-robot operation.
challenge: Field robots need perception that remains useful amid visually complex outdoor scenes. Cameras provide rich appearance cues, while mmWave radar contributes range and motion measurements unavailable from an image alone.
overview: I helped build a sensor-fusion pipeline for robots operating in agricultural field environments. The software combines YOLOv8 visual detections with radar measurements, projects radar observations into camera coordinates, and associates radar points with detected targets.
contributions: Built a YOLOv8-based visual detection pipeline and integrated it with radar measurements.
Worked on camera calibration and projection from radar coordinates into the image plane.
Implemented nearest-neighbor association between projected radar observations and visual targets.
Developed a usable visualization workflow for inspecting detections and radar data together.
workflow: Detect
Run object detection on camera images to identify candidate targets.
Align
Calibrate and project radar returns into the image coordinate system.
Associate
Match the complementary sensor observations to augment detections with radar information.
takeaway: The project strengthened my understanding of how calibration, temporal behavior, and sensor-specific failure modes affect a real perception system.

title: Autonomous Marine Vehicle Navigation & Control
summary: Developing an RRT path planner and validating an autonomous model boat through iterative field testing.
challenge: A path that looks valid in a simulator can fail on water, where heading dynamics, actuator response, and positioning uncertainty complicate the connection between planning and motion.
overview: For a team project building an autonomous surface vehicle, I led the RRT planning component and participated in integrating planning with a heading-control system. The team built and tested a differential-thrust boat equipped with positioning and inertial sensors.
contributions: Developed the RRT-based path planner in Python, including path refinement and parameter tuning.
Participated in integration with the team's guidance and PID-based tracking workflow.
Helped evaluate navigation runs and tune behavior using path deviation, time, and trajectory metrics.
Contributed to iterative field validation across 13 on-water test runs.
workflow: Plan
Create a collision-aware route from map obstacles with a sampling-based RRT planner.
Track
Convert the planned route into a heading reference and generate control commands through the team's tracking controller.
Validate
Run water tests, measure deviations, and refine planning/control settings.
takeaway: My primary ownership was the RRT path planner; guidance and control were collaborative parts of the larger vehicle system.

title: Toroidal Propeller Design & Hydrodynamic Optimization
summary: Pairing parametric geometry generation with CFD to investigate efficient toroidal propeller designs.
challenge: Unconventional propeller geometry introduces a complex design space: changing blade and ring geometry affects hydrodynamic loading, manufacturability, and propulsion efficiency.
overview: I developed software to generate and visualize toroidal propeller geometry, then studied how key parameters influence open-water hydrodynamic performance using Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes (RANS) simulation. The work resulted in a conference publication.
contributions: Developed a PyQt5 + VTK parametric geometry tool for 3D toroidal propeller modeling and export.
Set up and ran STAR-CCM+ CFD simulations to compare geometric configurations.
Conducted mesh-independence checks and comparisons against a conventional propeller baseline.
Analyzed the relationships among geometric design parameters and simulated hydrodynamic performance.
workflow: Parameterize
Generate blade surfaces and ring geometry from editable geometric parameters.
Simulate
Evaluate open-water behavior in STAR-CCM+ with RANS and a moving reference frame.
Compare
Validate numerical settings and compare performance metrics with the baseline design.
takeaway: The performance improvement refers to CFD results under the studied conditions—not a claimed measured sea-trial gain.
